analysis.one_liner: Restores lower capital gains tax rates and lets investors adjust asset costs for inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors and zero committee actions, dying in the House Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would undo part of the 1986 tax reform by putting capital gains — profits from selling stocks, business property, and similar assets — back into a special, lower-tax category: individuals would pay a 20 percent rate with 60 percent of long-term gains excluded from income, and corporations would pay 28 percent. It would also let sellers of stock and business property held more than a year raise their cost basis by inflation, so price increases caused by inflation would not be taxed as profit. The change would apply to sales after December 31, 1988.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and corporations that sell stocks or appreciated business property would pay significantly less tax. Because capital gains income is concentrated among wealthier taxpayers, the biggest winners would be high-income investors. Investment and financial services firms would also benefit, since lower rates reduce the tax penalty for selling assets and would encourage more trading and asset-management business.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Wealthy investors selling stocks and business assets

how_it_helps.text: Restores the pre-1986 treatment of capital gains: individuals would pay a 20 percent rate with a 60 percent deduction for long-term gain, and corporations would pay 28 percent on gains rather than the full corporate rate.

Lets sellers of corporate stock and tangible business property held more than one year increase their cost basis by inflation, measured by the gross national product deflator, so gains that merely reflect rising prices would not be taxed.
Applies to dispositions after December 31, 1988, so investors who had already sold assets since that date would qualify for the lower tax.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury would collect less revenue, because gains would be taxed at 20 percent instead of ordinary income rates and inflation adjustments would shrink taxable gains. That gap would eventually be covered through other taxes, spending cuts, or borrowing, spreading the cost across everyone else. Households with little or no investment income would get almost nothing from the bill.

drawbacks.text: The rate cut and inflation indexing would reduce federal revenue, since capital gains would be taxed at 20 percent instead of the ordinary income rates that the 1986 reform applied to them, and indexing would erase part of the taxable gain itself.

The benefits would flow mainly to the small share of households that own appreciated stock and business property, while the lost revenue would have to be made up by other taxpayers, other spending cuts, or more borrowing — a shift from broadly-based taxation toward tax advantages for asset holders.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would deliver a targeted tax cut to holders of stocks and business property, concentrated among high-income households, at the cost of federal revenue and a more complicated two-track tax system. For the majority of households with little taxable investment income, it offers no direct benefit, while the revenue loss would eventually have to be made up somewhere else in the tax code or the budget.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or vote there, and died when the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. David Dreier introduced the bill on May 16, 1989.
It was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee, which writes tax legislation, and no further action of any kind followed.
The bill attracted no cosponsors in the House.
When the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, the bill expired without a markup, a floor vote, or any action in the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much, because nothing happened. The post-1986 treatment of capital gains stayed in place and the Treasury kept the revenue the bill would have given up; investors hoping for the lower rate got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; the Treasury kept the revenue

for.name: Rep. David Dreier
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; no colleague joined as a cosponsor.

for.name: President George H.W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Pressed for cutting the capital gains tax rate in his 1989-90 budget agenda, backing the same goal as the bill, though through his own separate proposal.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill up in committee; it received no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes to measure, but the bill's only sponsor was a Republican, it drew zero cosponsors from either party, and the Democratic-led Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: High-income investors in stocks and business assets
industries.note: The bill would cut their tax rate to 20 percent, exclude 60 percent of long-term gains from income, and let them adjust their cost basis for inflation. Because gains are concentrated at the top of the income distribution, the tax cut and the revenue cost both land there, with the gap made up by everyone else.

Lower capital gains rates reduce the tax penalty for selling assets, which would encourage more trading and give brokerages and fund managers more fee business. The gain comes through a tax break for their wealthiest clients rather than any direct benefit to most households.

Corporations selling assets at a gain would pay 28 percent instead of the ordinary corporate rate the 1986 reform imposed, and would also get inflation indexing on business property. The revenue cost would be borne by the Treasury.
